extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of natural philosophy / scientific method (readers of Bacon); historians of science
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing decisive experiments ('instantiae crucis') and related instance-types (bivium, divortii, comitatus) to investigate the 'natures' of phenomena by Baconian induction. Covers general methodological rules and many concrete example-experiments for specific natural questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instantiae Crucis (crucial instances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances which dispose of rival hypotheses by yielding a decisive result about a nature; used to resolve questions about the true constitution or cause of a phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer experiments or observations which, if observed, would decisively favour one alternative and exclude the other. The text gives multiple examples of such 'instantiae crucis' (needles/terrella, clocks at different heights, comet motions, etc.). Note that a crucial instance can refute a rival hypothesis even if it does not by itself prove Bacon's own positive account; design them to directly discriminate between alternatives rather than rely on probable reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame the problem as a Bivium (two exhaustive alternatives) before testing
rubrics_metrics.description: When investigating a nature, pose the principal alternative (bivium) — typically two mutually exclusive accounts of the cause or constitution — and seek an instance to decide between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bivium examples: for 'pondus' (weight) either bodies tend to Earth's centre by their own nature or are attracted by Earth's mass; for magnetism either magnet impresses verticality on iron or the earth produces the verticality. If no decisive instance is found, the theory must be regarded as suspect and other crucial instances sought. Ensure the alternatives are stated sufficiently exhaustively; otherwise a decisive instance may only disprove one alternative (see unilateral-test caution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor experiments lucifera (light-bearing experiments) over 'probable' reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Use experiments that directly manifest the nature under question (experiments lucifera) rather than rely on probable arguments or abstract reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer treatment and concrete experimental protocols are provided so readers learn to judge nature by crucial instances and illuminating experiments, not by plausible-sounding but inconclusive reasoning. Many concrete experimental set-ups are described to make the 'nature' visible (e.g., needles on terrella, horologia at altitude/depth, flame colour experiments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware unilateral tests (they can be inconclusive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tests that, if positive, prove a hypothesis but, if negative, prove nothing (or vice versa) are limited and must be recognized as such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: showing that the Moon reflects light from solids would, if true, support the Moon being solid; showing that non-solids reflect light too would not prove the Moon is not solid. The text labels such single-direction tests 'unilateral' and warns they only dispose the issue one way and often leave the other hypothesis unproven.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Instances Divortii (instances of separation) to show that natures can be separated
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances that indicate separations of one nature from another (i.e., where properties normally conjoined are found apart) to prevent false generalizations and to dismantle naive conceptions from obvious resemblances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their use is to produce false forms and dissipate lightweight contemplations that arise from immediate resemblances. Examples given: Telesius' four natures (hot, luminous, tenuous, mobile) and many instances showing these qualities separate (e.g., air is tenuous and mobile but not hot or luminous). Instances Divortii differ from Instantiae Comitatus and Instantiae Hostiles in form and function; use them to test separability of attributes before asserting general identities of natures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish and use different kinds of instances appropriately (Comitatus, Hostiles, Divortii)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the different species of instances (comitatus, hostiles, divortii, etc.) and apply them according to their logical function in induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains distinctions: Instantiae Divortii indicate separations of natures from associated concretes; Instantiae Comitatus are separations of a nature from another concrete with which it commonly occurs; Instantiae Hostiles deny a nature of a concrete. Use the appropriate species to reveal separability, antagonisms, or supportive coincidences of natures in constructing inductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design a crucial instance to test planetary/comet motion hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: To test whether a comet's proper motion is 'rotational with the heavens' or opposed to the apparent diurnal motion, seek a concrete historical or observational instance where a comet moved contrary to the heavens' diurnal motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an observed comet is found that does not partake of the apparent diurnal motion but moves contrary (so visibly moves opposite to heavens), it would be an instance crucis settling the question. If no such instance is found, the theory remains suspect and other crucial instances must be sought. (Example used to challenge Bacon's skepticism about formal astronomy.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment to test the nature of 'weight' (gravity) using horologia at altitude vs subterranean
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare clocks moved by leaden weights placed at the summit of a high building and another in a deep mine to detect changes in the force of weights with distance from Earth's centre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: take a weight-driven clock ('horologium') and another driven by a different principle; place one clock high and another deep underground and note whether the high clock runs slower (diminished virtue of weights) and the subterranean one faster (increased virtue). If weights diminish aloft and increase in mines, accept terrestrial attraction as cause. The commentary notes physical laws (inverse-square outside a sphere, direct dependence inside) that affect results and that Bacon was right in expecting slower clocks higher up but wrong about deeper mines. This entry illustrates designing experiments where measurable effects (clock rates) discriminate between alternative accounts of 'weight.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Terrella / needle experiment to decide magnetism vs earth-cause of needle verticality
rubrics_metrics.description: Place a small magnetized 'terrella' with its poles oriented east–west, lay an unmagnetized iron needle on it and after days remove the needle and put it on a versorium to see whether it resumes orientation to Earth's poles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the needle, removed from the magnet and placed on a pivot, immediately turns to the Earth's north–south, infer that Earth's presence causes verticality; if it continues to point east–west or loses verticality, regard Earth's presence as suspect and investigate further. The procedure is given in detail (leave the iron for six or seven days on the terrella, then remove and test on a versorium) showing a concrete crucial-instance design for magnetism questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tests for the lunar substance (solid vs tenuous) via reflection and flame experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: To test whether the Moon's substance is tenuous (flame/air-like) or solid/dense, seek instances that demonstrate reflection from tenuous bodies of sufficient thickness or more telling optical experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested experiments: investigate reflection of sunlight from upper air (cause of twilight), observe sunlight reflected by cloud edges at evening, test transmission of rays through a hole onto an obscurer/blue flame to see whether the flame reflects or appears like smoke. Note the caution that reflection is not unique to solids and that such instances may disprove a specific argument but not prove the affirmative. Also suggests attempting to transmit rays through a hole to a flame to see effects on appearance (flame may appear like white smoke), and notes general optical principle that incident rays are either reflected, transmitted, or absorbed (unknown to Bacon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment to discriminate theories of projectile motion (air-driven vs inherent motion)
rubrics_metrics.description: To decide whether the continued motion of projectiles is due to the air carrying them or to parts of the projectile itself continuing motion, use a thin blade, wire, reed, or feather split in the middle and curved between thumb and finger to observe where the source of motion lies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bivium: either motion is produced by the moving external medium (air) carrying the projectile like a stream, or by parts of the projectile itself transmitting motion by internal succession. The lamina/filum/calamus experiment shows the source is in the middle (not carried by air), contradicting purely external-air explanations. The commentary also cautions that Bacon did not frame the problem exactly: the modern question is why motion ceases, not how it is continued. Use experimental designs that reveal loci of motion (middle vs extremes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiments to investigate explosive expansion of gunpowder (intrinsic expansion vs eruption of 'crude spirit')
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether the violent expansion of gunpowder on ignition is due to intrinsic appetite of the solid to dilate on burning or to the escape of a crude spirit (gas) that violently erupts, compare materials that readily take flame with those that repel flame and observe eruption/expansion behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bivium: expansion caused by the body's own appetite to dilate once inflamed, or caused by a crude spirit in a component (e.g., nitre) that flees from fire. Suggested instances: compare strongly inflammable mixtures (sulphur, camphor, naphtha) which readily generate flame with salts that repel flame (salts that erupt aqueous spirit such as quicksilver/mercury? — text cites 'aqua mineralis' behaviour) and note whether eruption/expansion occurs before flame generation. The text recommends observing species that emit spirit and expand (e.g., some salts) and notes later chemical explanation: sudden development of large volumes of gas (N2, CO2) explains explosive force — but the methodological point is designing discriminating experiments to test competing causal accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiments probing the transitory (momentary) nature of flame and its extinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Test whether an observed continuous flame is the same individual flame persisting, or a succession of momentary flames; and whether extinction is due to loss of the generating cause or to destructive influences of surrounding natures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bivium: flame is transient (momentary generations each instant) or the same flame persists but is destroyed by surrounding contrary natures. Suggested crucial instances: observe flame shape and height in large fires (wider base yields higher vertex); consider that extinction begins at sides where air compresses and poorly supports flame. Concrete experimental design: create bicoloured flames (small metal cup with a candle and a little spirit of wine around it) and note whether the lamp-flame remains pyramidal or tends to spherical when enclosed by another flame; also test whether a flame enclosed within another remains 'the same number' (i.e., same continued individual) as long as it is protected from hostile air. Use such experiments to infer the role of surrounding air and competing constituents in flame persistence or extinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use many and diverse crucial instances, not single examples, and learn to judge nature by them
rubrics_metrics.description: Longer, repeated, and diversified instances are needed so people learn to judge nature by crucial instances and illuminating experiments rather than by plausible but untested reasonings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author emphasizes giving long treatment of crucial instances so that readers become habituated to judging nature by experiments and instances crucis and experiments lucifera. Use multiple instances across conditions (height, depth, different materials, different enclosures) to avoid hasty generalization and to uncover separability of attributes.
